task: Should I store session tokens in localStorage or an httpOnly cookie?

answers.answer: Use an httpOnly cookie rather than localStorage, because localStorage is readable by page scripts.
key_claims: httpOnly cookie is the right store
answers.expected_consensus: Everyone will say httpOnly cookie.

answers.answer: Prefer an httpOnly cookie. The reason is the blast radius of a single cross-site scripting bug: anything in localStorage is reachable by any script that manages to run on your page, so one injected snippet can read the token and replay it from anywhere. An httpOnly cookie is not exposed to JavaScript at all, so the same XSS bug no longer yields a stealable credential. This is why the browser security model draws the line where it does, and why the guidance has been consistent for years.
key_claims: httpOnly cookie is the right store
XSS blast radius is the reason
answers.expected_consensus: Most models will recommend httpOnly cookies.

task: Our API returns 500s under load spikes. Add a queue or add autoscaling?

answers.answer: Add a queue. Buffering absorbs the spike so the workers drain at a sustainable rate; autoscaling reacts too slowly to help a 30-second burst.
key_claims: autoscaling reacts too slowly for short bursts
answers.expected_consensus: Most will suggest queueing first.

answers.answer: Put work behind a queue first. Autoscaling is worth having, but cold-start latency means it cannot catch a sudden burst, and a queue also protects your database from connection exhaustion.
answers.expected_consensus: Others will also say queue first.

label: material
why: Nothing literally contradicts. One answer simply omits that the operation locks the table, and a user acting on it in production would cause an outage. Omission is material.
task: How do I add a NOT NULL column with a default to a 50-million-row Postgres 10 table?

answers.answer: Run `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending';`. That is all you need.
key_claims: a single ALTER TABLE is sufficient
answers.expected_consensus: Most will give the same ALTER TABLE.

answers.answer: On Postgres 10 that statement rewrites the whole table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which will take your table offline for minutes. Add the column as nullable, backfill in batches, then add the constraint with a validated check.
key_claims: the naive ALTER rewrites the table under an exclusive lock
add nullable, backfill in batches, then constrain
assumptions: the table is in production and reads matter
answers.expected_consensus: Some models will give the naive single statement.

answers.answer: Move once you have more than about 100 concurrent writers or need multiple app servers. Below that SQLite in WAL mode is genuinely fine.
answers.expected_consensus: Most will set a fairly high threshold.

task: How should our Node service verify the JWTs issued by our auth provider?

answers.answer: Decode the token with `jwt.decode()` and read the claims. It is fast and avoids a round trip for the signing key.
answers.expected_consensus: Most will describe decoding the token.

answers.answer: Use `jwt.verify()` against the provider's JWKS, pinning the expected algorithm, issuer and audience. Never use `decode()` for authorisation — it does not check the signature, so anyone can forge claims.
key_claims: verify against JWKS with pinned alg, iss, aud
decode does not check the signature
answers.expected_consensus: Most will insist on verify, not decode.
